summary:
COSMIC LEGACY – Every Machine Has a Story. Every Discovery Leaves a Legacy.

COSMIC LEGACY is an interactive, browser-based 3D storytelling and learning platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Inspired by the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars,”the project brings the history of space exploration equipment to life using information and resources from NASA's published mission records and official materials.

Through an immersive 3D solar system, users can explore 13 artifact entries across three categories: Moon and Mars. Each discovery presents mission histories, equipment details, scientific contributions, and historical facts based on NASA resources. The platform combines interactive 3D exploration, voice narration, quizzes, mini-games, and an AI-assisted mission information experience.

Built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js, COSMIC LEGACY transforms authentic space exploration information into an engaging and accessible digital learning experience.
details:
Here is a comprehensive breakdown of Cosmic Legacy by Team TechTitanz for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing each of your questions based on the presentation:

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Cosmic Legacy is a browser-based interactive 3D platform that tells the stories of NASA's discarded and inactive spacecraft, rovers, and equipment left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space.

Users follow a five-step interactive workflow:

  1. Interactive 3D Solar System: Explore planetary models in a 3D environment.
  2. Artifact Selection: Browse 13 artifact entries categorized across three exploration zones (such as the Moon, Mars, and deep space).
  3. Mission Info & 3D Inspection: Inspect detailed spacecraft models with interactive camera controls. Users can toggle an Exploded View (using a separation slider and leader lines to inspect individual hardware parts like gold foil, plaques, and retroreflectors), switch to a First-Person perspective, check simulated or live Space Weather and Mission Ops telemetry, and query the built-in Mission AI assistant about mission histories and statuses.
  4. Narration & Quizzes: Listen to mission stories via an integrated voice narration engine and play interactive quizzes and mini-games.
  5. Points & Certificate: Track progress locally to earn points, badges, and a completion certificate.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Because it runs directly in a web browser without requiring specialized software or high-end installations, students anywhere can explore space artifacts easily.
  • Active Hands-On Learning: Instead of reading static text archives, learners visually dissect spacecraft components, test their knowledge through mini-games, and ask questions directly to Mission AI.
  • Multi-Sensory Engagement: Combining 3D visual exploration, text-to-speech audio narration, and gamified rewards accommodates different learning styles.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The project aims to transform the overlooked remnants of space missions from forgotten hardware into an unforgettable educational journey. Specifically, it intends to:

  • Democratize access to authentic NASA mission histories and landing coordinates for students worldwide.
  • Spark curiosity and encourage self-directed exploration of space engineering.
  • Inspire the next generation of space explorers by preserving the legacy of humanity's milestones beyond Earth.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • 3D Graphics & Rendering: Three.js for browser-based 3D rendering, planetary scenes, exploded-view assembly mechanics, and interactive camera controls.
  • Browser APIs & Engines: HTML5 Canvas for interactive mini-games, the Web Speech / browser text-to-speech engine for voice narration, and browser local storage for progress tracking.
  • Data Architecture: A structured spacecraft and mission database powering the 13 artifact profiles, telemetry displays, and Mission AI responses.
  • Hardware: Standard consumer computers/browsers capable of WebGL rendering (no specialized VR or external hardware required for end users).

5. How is your project creative?

  • Reframing "Space Junk" as Storytelling: Rather than focusing only on active launches, the project humanizes abandoned hardware—treating silent rovers, lunar modules, and probes as historical monuments with personal stories.
  • Interactive Engineering Dissection: Including an adjustable Exploded View with component-by-component percentages and leader lines blends museum-style storytelling with CAD-like engineering inspection.
  • Simulated Mission Context: Integrating a Mission Ops dashboard with live/simulated space weather (solar wind speed, geomagnetic Kp index) and an interactive Mission AI makes users feel like active flight controllers rather than passive readers.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility & Performance: Building a lightweight browser-based stack (vanilla JS + Three.js) ensures smooth performance on standard student laptops without downloads.
  • Educational Engagement & Retention: To prevent information overload, the team balanced technical mission data with audio narration, interactive quizzes, mini-games, and a certificate reward system.
  • Historical & Technical Accuracy: Structuring authentic NASA mission details—such as exact landing coordinates, mission end dates, component breakdowns, and realistic space weather telemetry—ensures the platform serves as a credible educational resource.
  • User Experience (UX) & Navigation: Designing clear camera transitions (from solar system overview to first-person surface view and exploded hardware view) keeps complex 3D navigation intuitive for first-time users.
